text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The board of national railway company SJ and the Swedish Communications Ministry have demanded that SJ explain why it secretly attempted to lobby for higher taxes on company cars used by employees. SJ's secret campaign was uncovered by the newspaper on Wednesday.
- The Swedish labour market cannot agree about how wages should be set. Prime Minister Goran Persson has asked employers and unions to agree on a solution by March 31.

- Lars Tingstrom, the so called Bomb Man, told a journalist about two months before he died in 1993 that he did not have any intentions to take revenge on society. The lawyer Pelle Svensson recently told media that Tingstrom on his deathbed said he had planned the murder of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme in 1986.

- Everything indicates that Swedish telecoms group Ericsson will keep selling non-core businesses. This week Ericsson announced it would restructure its Norrkoping plant and outsource printed board manufacturing, affecting 1,400 jobs.

- The minority Social Democratic government is far from reaching its target of cutting unemployment to four percent in the year 2000, government think tank KI forecast on Wednesday. KI expects unemployment to fall to 8.3 percent in 1997 and to seven percent in 2000.
Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said, however, that the government will implement further measures to increase employment.
- The Swedish secret service has intervened several times to stop Swedish companies from exporting technical components to illegal nuclear weapons projects in other countries, a report showed.

- The southern Swedish town of Jonkoping is breaking the naitonal labour market trend. Some 26 percent more jobs materialised there in the first two months of the year compared to the same period last year.

- Sweden's two largest tabloids, Expressen and Aftonbladet, are knocking themselves out financially in trying to compete with costly late editions. Expressen owner Marieberg has invested 40 million crowns in the project, which was quickly imitated by Aftonbladet. But Expressen's circulation has increased by only 4,000 to 8,000 newspapers, according to Dagens Industri's sources, which means that the newspaper might be losing as much as 800,000 crowns a week.
- Sweden's economy will grow by two percent this year and by 2.5 percent next year, government think tank KI forecast.
